narrative:
The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution against investing in someone who might soon depart.

The decision was driven mainly by three factors. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence, but it pulled the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. Most employees the model expects to remain have similar short experience levels, so this actually worked in your favor. What pushed the prediction upward instead were the other two key factors. Having received other job offers while at your current company was the second most important reason, strongly increasing the likelihood of leaving; only about one in four employees predicted to stay report receiving such external opportunities. Third, working in the “other” sector also nudged the prediction toward departure. While this sector represents just over one-fifth of employees the model expects to stay, it appears associated with higher turnover in the broader patterns the system has learned.

Taken together, these elements outweighed the positive signal from your experience and produced a prediction that tilts toward leaving. The organization should discuss with you whether those external offers remain active and explore ways to strengthen your sense of long-term fit here. You may want to reflect on what would make staying more attractive before considering your next career step. (248 words)
